audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on p.3 of the OPD PDF we hold, both the 'Stress is contrastive' line with the two minimal pairs and 'Phonemic stress is not written'. (2) The deciding source is a 4-page unrefereed SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (2001/2004) by the long-term fieldworker; first-hand but minimal (one sentence, two pairs, no statement of default position). Glottolog's two descriptive refs add nothing on stress: Hynum 2010 (downloaded, PL 616) is silent; Hynum 1995 grammar notes (177 pp ms) is archive-only. No published phonology, dissertation or instrumental study of Numanggang exists per web search. (3) The one open work that bears on the classification, Pennington 2014 (downloaded), explicitly disputes the 'contrastive' reading of túo/tuót as weight-driven shift from default initial stress, in line with every described Erap relative (Nek, Finongan, Uri, Ma Manda: word-initial, quality/quanti

sources.citation: Pennington, Ryan. 2014 [MA thesis GIAL 2013]. Ma Manda Phonology. SIL e-Books 64. Dallas: SIL International. 220 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Related Erap languages Nek, Finongan, and Uri have also been analyzed as having versions of word-initial quality-sensitive stress systems ... Regarding closely-related Numanggang, Hynum (2001:3) claims that stress is contrastive. However, the examples provided suggest a similar behavior to that of Ma Manda. For instance, a pair is given: túo 'firstborn son' and tuót 'enough'. It is quite clear that a heavy second syllable is attracting the stress. This is seen in the comparable Ma Manda pair: túwə 'firstborn son' and tuwóŋ 'firstborn son.3SG:POSS'.'
